chapter_theme: At the wedding of the Ilakkanaiyar ilampakam the city is heaped with goods and decked with flags and pots, the astrologer fixes the hour, the king is bathed by elephant-borne water and anointed with ghee amid blessings, then dressed, perfumed and fanned by countless fly-whisks.

cast.role: the hero, bridegroom of the Ilakkanaiyar ilampakam
the bride of the ilampakam (named only in its title)
the astrologer who fixes the auspicious hour
the women who attend, bathe, anoint and bless
the kings who attend the rite
the townspeople who lay out the festival
the thousand and eight who raise fly-whisks
the guards who wave the fly-whisks

2403.reading: The city heaps up areca bunches, tender betel leaves, camphor and the rest in such quantity that the great earth can scarcely bear them, for people to take freely and eat.
2403.nuance: The lavishness is the point: the goods are laid out as plunder (கொள்ளை) to be taken, so the wedding feast is open to all.
2403.event: The townspeople pile up areca, betel and camphor for all to take.

2404.reading: Heaps of incense-smoking luxuries, held up as good fortune, make the fine city look as if the golden wish-trees and the wish-creeper had taken it as their ground.

2405.reading: The earth-maiden, unable to bear the crowd of people and cattle, is imagined opening her whole mouth and weeping, her tears turning into ghee and milk.
2405.nuance: A conceit of plenty: the earth's weight of people and herds becomes a flood of ghee and milk. This is the poet's figure, not a doctrinal claim about the earth.

2406.reading: At the palace gates the banners rise, areca and plantain put out their spathes, and mirrors, silks and full auspicious pots stand in bloom.
2406.nuance: The auspicious objects (flags, pots full of water, mirrors, areca and plantain) are named as the marks of a wedding house; the verse gives no event.

2407.reading: In the palace where women's anklets and bells ring, a wealth is said to have filled the place that the umbrella-shaded kings had not found on earth.
2407.nuance: The last two lines (கோதைத் தாதுவேய்த் தடிநிலம் பெறாததோர் செல்வம்) are hard to construe; the sense of 'wealth the kings did not find on earth' is the likeliest.

2408.reading: Ear-ornaments, studs, powder, aloe paste and flowers, with gem ornaments and necklaces throwing young rays, shine so that they make the upper world seem to be spurned.
2408.nuance: The hyperbole (the heaven-dwellers' world made loathsome beside this display) is the epic's habitual way of praising a festival.

2409.reading: The city, built like the waist of the goddess of the golden lotus and roofed like a sky blossomed with gem-dust, is made ready as the garlanded people set the great auspicious seat.
2409.nuance: தவிசு is read as the seat on which the rite is done; the verse does not say who will sit on it.
2409.event: The garlanded people set up the great auspicious seat.

2410.reading: Gold, gems and conch pearls are heaped as auspicious offerings, lamps burn and sweet smoke rises, and one thousand and eight attendants raise fly-whisks.
2410.event: Attendants raise fly-whisks among the heaped auspicious wealth.

2411.reading: After the great astrologer fixes the hour, the auspicious king mounts, rice grains are sprinkled, auspicious instruments sound before him, and he is blessed with true words.
2411.nuance: Line 2's வேறலு is not clear (perhaps ஏறலு, 'on mounting'); the whole verse is read as the beginning of the rite at the hour the astrologer set.
2411.event: The astrologer's hour is fixed, and the king is blessed with rice grains and music.

2412.reading: As auspicious instruments sound with a sweet roar, women with plump carp-like eyes take golden vessels and go down to the bath for the sacred hair, while rows of fly-whisks gleam and conchs boom.
2412.nuance: திருமயிர் is taken as the hair of the one to be bathed; whether it is the bridegroom's or the bride's is not said in this verse.
2412.event: Carp-eyed women go down with golden vessels to the bath as instruments sound.

2413.reading: The gold-garlanded woman, bright like a coral creeper sprung from the milk-sea, is given her day's fragrant hair-dressing so that the goddess who dwells in the golden lotus is left to lament.
2413.nuance: The woman is taken to be Lakshanai, the bride of the ilampakam's title, though she is not named; the closing figure says her beauty leaves the lotus-goddess grieving.

2414.reading: Garlands are set on, the women's palms redden, and one thousand and eight elephants, their tusks smeared with ground sandal, are lined up for the bathing water, drums booming and rut-water wetting the ground like mountain spray.
2414.event: A thousand and eight sandal-marked elephants are drawn up for the bathing water amid drums.

2415.reading: Spear-eyed women raise golden pots of clear water onto the elephants' heads while the people stare as at a moon among confused stars, and fortune is given under the garlanded umbrella's shade.
2415.nuance: The last line (குடைநிழற் றிருவிற் றந்தார்) can be read as the giving of fortune under the umbrella or as a naming of the pots; I take the first.
2415.event: Women lift the golden pots of bathing water onto the elephants' heads.

2416.reading: When the king, ear-rings flashing, has sat on the silver seat while kings praise him, women dip durva grass in ghee and anoint him with it.
2416.event: The king sits on a silver seat and women anoint him with ghee on durva.

2417.reading: Women bless him as they pour ghee: may he shine on earth like the Himalaya of diamond peaks, may the world lie in the shade of his feet, and may he be lord of the wheel and abide with Fortune.
2417.nuance: The blessing wishes sovereignty over the whole earth (நேமியஞ் செல்வன்), a wish, not a fact in the story; it is spoken to the bridegroom, not to a king already crowned.
2417.event: Women bless the king as they anoint him with ghee.

2418.reading: The women like lightning rub and bathe him with water of gems and with perfumed waters, and instruments sound together.
2418.event: Women rub and bathe the king amid music.

2419.reading: The water the chariot-kings pour from silver pots over the fortunate king's head looks like the moon's sweet rays pouring down when the sun's light is hidden.
2419.nuance: The kings serve the bridegroom with the water of the bath, so the vassal kings of the earlier chapters now do him honour in the rite.
2419.event: The chariot-kings pour water from silver pots over the king's head.

2420.reading: A pavilion of gem is raised on four shining gem pillars, silver-roofed and ringed with garlands, so that it looks like the young sun resting there.
2420.event: Attendants set up a gem pavilion on four pillars with a silver roof.

2421.reading: A rug of golden milk-white wool is spread on the white-gold dais under a pearl canopy, and the seat is made ready for him.
2421.nuance: Line 4 (கேந்தினார் அணி ஏந்தும் நீர்மையால்) is unclear in the printed text.

2422.reading: When the damp has been dried, his hair, from which the dark gem-light spreads shadow, is scented with aloe smoke until it looks painted.
2422.event: Attendants dry and scent his hair with aloe smoke.

2423.reading: He anoints himself with matchless sandal and puts on a bee-loud garland whose pure flowers seem to have won release that day.
2423.nuance: வீடு பெற்றன is a figure for flowers that are lucky to be worn; it makes no claim about release and is not a doctrinal use of veedu.
2423.event: He anoints himself with sandal and puts on a garland.

2424.reading: On his broad chest the necklace casts a rainbow, as if the wishing tree had blossomed, and he wears gold ornaments.
2424.event: He puts on his gold ornaments and necklace.

2425.reading: In hair-silk and with flashing ear-rings and a garland like Indra's bow, he becomes Kama himself to the women of fragrant hair.
2425.event: He dresses in silk and ornaments and looks like Kama to the women.

2426.reading: After the hanging garlands shine and water and rice grains are sprinkled, they wave incense smoke and show the unwavering fierce lamps.
2426.event: Attendants sprinkle rice and water and wave incense and lamps.

2427.reading: The guards wave so many white whisks, like the sea's foam-white waves, that the count of them is lost.
2427.nuance: The last line (இவரித் தொகை என்பது இன்றி ஆயினார்) is taken to mean that the whisks passed counting.

links.note: The city's wealth is compared to a grove of wish-granting trees with honey-dripping garlands and ambrosia in the first ilampakam; here the festival goods held up in incense smoke make the city look as if the golden wish-trees and the wish-creeper had taken it.
links.teaches: The same wishing-tree figure that praised a city's standing wealth is now used for the wealth brought out for a wedding, so the epic's image of plenty follows the occasion.

links.note: The wedding instruments sound and the carp-eyed women go to the bath; the Naladiyar quatrain says the drums that sounded as wedding drums may sound that day in that place as funeral drums for the bridegroom.
links.teaches: The epic gives the drums only their joyful sound, and the quatrain reminds the reader that a hero's wedding festival is not yet a safe ground for pride, which matters in a poem that ends with its hero leaving the throne.

gains.a: The festival's drums and blessings, which the verse sounds only for joy, gain the warning that the same drums can turn funereal, which the verse never says.
gains.b: The quatrain's general rule gains a long, fully dressed wedding of a hero who will later fear kingship, so the lesson meets a concrete story.

links.note: The king reads Vijayai's dream of the shoot and crown as her son's rising fortune; at the ghee-anointing the women now bless him to be lord of the wheel and to abide with Fortune.
links.teaches: The fortune that the king foretold from the dream is voiced as a blessing in the rite, so the reader sees the prophecy being fulfilled step by step.

links.note: After the cattle-raid the women wished that the young elephant of a man wed the earth too; at the anointing they now wish that he be wheel-lord and live in Fortune.
links.teaches: The earlier, offhand wish for him to wed the earth returns as a formal blessing in a rite, so the epic marks how far his standing has risen since the cattle-raid.

links.note: After the last battle he is called a Kama even to the wise as he sits like a lion in his silk; at the wedding bath he again becomes Kama to the women of fragrant hair.
links.teaches: The poet gives the hero the Kama figure in victory and again in his wedding dress, so the epic ties his beauty first to conquest and then to marriage.

links.note: The guards wave countless whisks and the festival's wealth is beyond count; the poem's summary says that while kings brought tribute and fortune stayed, Civakan heard the dharma, feared kingship like a snake struck by thunder, and renounced.
links.teaches: Read with the closing renunciation, the countless whisks mark the height of the splendour he will later flee, so the poem's praise of kingship is held against its end.

source_issues: 2414-2417 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2405 line 3 மண்மகண் is probably a misprint for மண்மகள்; line 1 வழுவின் may stand for வழுவில்.
2407 lines 3-4 (தடிநிலம் பெறாததோர்) are hard to construe.
